sources.title: Historical constitutional periods of Peru
sources.institution: Congress of Peru
sources.usage: Read full dated index: 1860 charter restored January 1868, interrupted 27 December 1879 by Pierola statute through 18 January 1881, restored later 1883–1920. Not an uninterrupted 1860–1920 constitution.

sources.title: Constitution of Peru, 1860, annotated historical text
sources.institution: Congress of Peru
sources.usage: Read primary Articles 42–44,78: unitary representative republic, Senate and Deputies, President. Dated later amendments excluded from earlier details; legal provisions not blanket democratic-practice claims.

sources.title: Provisional Statute of Peru, 27 December 1879
sources.institution: Congress of Peru
sources.usage: Read all three primary pages: Pierola Supreme Chief, consultative Council of State and wartime clauses. Not ordinary bicameral/presidential continuation.

sources.title: Constitution of Uruguay, 1830
sources.institution: Parliament of Uruguay Library
sources.usage: Read primary Articles 13–16 and executive chapter: representative republic, three powers, bicameral Assembly and President. Restricted citizenship clauses not unrestricted democracy.

sources.title: Uruguay executive historical evolution
sources.institution: Presidency of Uruguay
sources.usage: Read body: 1830 President, 1918 dual President and Council, 31 March 1933 rupture, 1934/1942 ministers and presidency, 1952 collegiate Council replaces President. Modern 1967 structure and official 1934 democracy claim excluded.

sources.title: Uruguay Parliament historical account
sources.institution: Parliament of Uruguay
sources.usage: Read body: bicameral structure, 1918 changes, 1933 interruption and 1934 chambers, 1952 nine-member executive. Contradictory 1942 coup chronology not used for precise dates.

sources.title: Venezuela: caudillismo
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read full body: Guzman predominance 1870–1888, Castro 1899–1908, Gomez dictatorship 1908–1935 despite changes in formal offices. Practical rulers not assigned continuous formal presidency.

sources.title: Venezuela: transition to civilian rule
sources.institution: US Library of Congress, Federal Research Division; historical Country Study text mirror
sources.usage: Read full historical body: Lopez 1936–1941, Medina bicameral Congress 1943–1945, 18 October 1945 coup and Betancourt junta; 1946 suffrage not applied to 1945; Betancourt inauguration 13 February 1959 and elected bicameral Congress. No 1961 constitution in 1960.

historicalCautions: Kingdom of Brazil raw 1878/1880/1900 resolves to independently evidenced Empire/Republic; actual late-1815 kingdom separately mapped.
Brazil 1815 and Venezuela 1945 retain multiple identities inside the requested calendar year.
Formal constitutional institutions do not establish unrestricted democratic practice or effective control across every polygon.
Peru 1880 is Pierola wartime administration, not ordinary bicameral/presidential continuation.
British Guiana is colonial and Suriname a Kingdom constituent country in 1960; no modern independent-state fallback.
New Granada 1815 Viceroyalty raw remains review because reconquest and revolutionary authority vary spatially.
End bounds delimit editorial coverage, not complete lifetimes; no automatic succession.

overviewPeriods.note: An overseas possession of the Portuguese monarchy, before the royal court transfer. A viceroyal snapshot label does not establish a named officeholder or exact territorial control.
After the 1808 court transfer, Brazil housed central monarchy institutions. This differs from ordinary viceroyal government; December 1815 elevation is separately dated.
The law of 16 December 1815 elevated Brazil alongside Portugal and the Algarves. This late-1815 interval neither asserts independence nor projects the later Empire backward.

The 1824 charter established legislative, moderating, executive and judicial powers. Pedro II ruled in this interval. Kingdom of Brazil in the raw dataset is not accepted as the contemporary polity name.

The 1891 charter provided a federal republic, President, Deputies and Senate. Curation stops before the 1930 overthrow and does not equate contemporary restricted participation with universal democracy.
Congress and state legislatures were dissolved; the legislature projected in the 1937 charter never operated. Vargas removal in October 1945 begins a separate interim framework.
The military appointed Supreme Court president Linhares after Vargas removal. This administration preceded the elected presidency and constituent legislature of 1946.

The 1946 settlement restored divided federal powers and Congress. Coverage starts in 1947 to avoid inconsistent commencement dates and ends before 1961 changes. Individual presidency and capital transitions remain uncurated.
Subordinate to Rio de la Plata after 1776, Paraguay provincial administration was distinct from a sovereign republic. Coverage precedes the disruptions culminating in 1811 independence.
The 1813 republic developed into Francia personal government from 1814. Exact annual-to-perpetual dictatorship dates are not invented.

The charter prescribed divided powers, President, Senate and Representatives. Formal provisions differed from strong executive practice; occupation details and individual administrations are uncurated.
The July 1940 charter concentrated executive power and replaced bicameral Congress. Constitutional guarantees are not asserted as democratic practice or exhaustive wartime government history.
Stroessner governed under the 1940 constitution while the state of siege introduced in 1954 was repeatedly renewed. The 1967 charter is excluded.
The historical charter prescribed a federal republic, President and Deputies and Senate. This formal core excludes later 1957 provisions, uncurated leaders and claims of unrestricted democracy.

The 1949 charter retained federal republican government and Deputies and Senate. Narrow 1950–1954 coverage excludes later overthrow and constitutional restoration; practical government details remain uncurated.

The charter established a unitary republic with restricted participation. This legal framework does not assert uninterrupted cabinet control or absence of coups. Curation stops before the new social charters.

A new social charter was adopted during the Villarroel regime of 1943–1946. This narrow 1945 profile does not import later institutions or characterize military-linked government as ordinary democracy.
The 1952 revolution changed practical authority and participation. Ratification of the earlier charter in 1956 differs from the new 1961 constitution, which remains excluded.
Liberal reforms modified the executive-centered charter. Coverage stops before the 1891 war and parliamentary practice; detailed cabinet and electoral records remain uncurated.

After 1891, parliamentary interpretation reduced executive power without an English-style replacement charter. Ministers answered to Congress and participation remained restricted. Curation stops before the 1924 intervention.

Presidential and congressional institutions resumed after the 1924–1932 disruptions. Authoritarian measures and coalition politics coexisted with the charter; the earlier Ibanez dictatorship is separately excluded.
The charter named United States of Colombia and reserved broad state powers. Weak federal authority and recurring conflict prevent claims of uniform central control across geometry.

The 1886 charter replaced the federal framework with a unified Republic. The 1899–1902 war contested authority; this profile describes constitutional organization rather than effective control throughout a polygon.
Lleras Camargo took office in August 1958 amid constitutional restoration. Narrow early coalition coverage excludes the prior military dictatorship and later state-of-siege governments.
The charter prescribed a presidential republic with bicameral Congress. Historical presidencies operated alongside coastal elite influence; coverage ends before the July 1925 coup.

Consecutive completed elected presidencies followed 1948, then Velasco return in 1960. The crisis and military overthrow of November 1961 are outside coverage. Modern details do not fill historical gaps.

French Guiana was a colony under governors. This status is not independent sovereignty. Coverage is editorially limited to 1878–1929; detailed inland subdivisions and territorial administration remain uncurated.
The law of 19 March 1946 converted the colony to a French department, followed by prefects. This does not establish independent sovereignty or resolve every special inland administrative arrangement.
Before the 1928 Crown Colony constitution, legislation operated through the Court of Policy. The dataset name Guyana does not imply independence in 1914 or 1920.
The 1928 constitution replaced the Court of Policy with a Legislative Council. Coverage ends before the elected bicameral system and constitutional suspension of 1953.

After the October 1953 suspension, interim provisions provided nominated bodies. Council dissolution on 29 June 1957 is separately bounded. An Order made date is not assumed commencement of every provision.
The successor to the June 1957 council combined elected, appointed and official members. New 1961 bicameral government and 1966 independence are not projected into colonial 1960.
The regulation effective in 1866 provided colonial representation and governor ordinances with Staten consent. Dutch Guiana is attested as a name for Suriname, not a separate sovereign state.
The 1954 settlement provided internal autonomy while defense and foreign affairs remained Kingdom matters. This differed from colonial status and from sovereign independence achieved in 1975.
Peru was a royalist base under viceroyal administration before the 1820 coastal independence campaign. Precise territorial control, individual tenures and republican succession are not inferred.
The earlier charter was restored in January 1868 after the brief 1867 constitution. Pierola takeover in December 1879 starts a distinct wartime framework.
Pierola statute displaced the previous constitutional arrangement during the Pacific War and provided a consultative Council. Effective wartime control is not equated with the entire raw polygon.

The congressional chronology records renewed charter operation after the war. This formal core stops before 1919–1920; coups, presidents and practical electoral restrictions are not exhaustively curated.

The charter prescribed a President and Assembly of Representatives and Senators. This later interval excludes earlier military governments; legal provisions are not unrestricted democratic participation.
The 1918 charter divided executive responsibilities between President and Council. Coverage starts after the transition and ends at the 31 March 1933 dissolution of chambers.
Presidency with ministers continued under the 1942 charter. Narrow post-transition coverage avoids contradictory coup dates in the institutional history and ends before the collegiate arrangement.
The 1952 constitution replaced the Presidency with a Council. Modern presidential government is not fallback in 1960; single-presidency restoration in 1967 is excluded.
Guzman dominated politics despite officeholder changes. Practical predominance is not an uninterrupted formal presidency or democratic parliamentary framework.
Castro exercised predominant government after taking power in 1899. Coverage stops before the 1908 transition; constitutional iterations and cabinet details remain uncurated.
Gomez retained political power while formal presidency and other offices changed. No continuous presidential tenure is invented; coverage stops before his death and 1935–1936 transition.
Some opening after Gomez coexisted with restrictions on organized opposition. Full-year coverage within this presidency does not characterize unrestricted democracy.
Medina expanded political organization and governed with Congress. His 18 October 1945 removal starts a separate junta; the whole year cannot resolve to a single government.
The coup installed a junta with civilian and military members. Adult suffrage enacted in 1946 and the 1947 charter are not imported into late 1945.
Inauguration on 13 February 1959 followed the 1958 election and coalition settlement. Prior dictatorship and new 1961 constitution are excluded.
Spanish viceroys governed from Buenos Aires after Viceroyalty creation in 1776. Pre-1806 coverage does not imply modern Argentine borders or automatic succession.

The May statute prescribed provisional executive and oversight arrangements, including provincial acceptance provisions. It is not the 1816 independence declaration or proof of obedience of every province.
